subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: S and T are the foci of an ellipse and B is one end of the minor axis. If STB is an equilateral triangle, then find the eccentricity of the ellipse.

mark_split.label: Name the three sides of the triangle

insider_note: Distance formulas for SB and TB both come out to √(a²e² + b²) automatically, since S and T are mirror images of each other about the minor axis — so only ST = SB needs to be set up, not ST = SB = TB separately.

steps.label: Name the three sides of the triangle
steps.margin_note: First mark. S, T are the two foci; B is one end of the minor axis.
steps.memory_tip: Foci are always (±ae, 0); the end of the minor axis is (0, b).
lines: Let the ellipse be x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, (a > b)
B(0, b) is one end of the minor axis
steps.why: The distance between the foci is 2ae, and SB (or TB) is found by the distance formula between a focus and the top of the minor axis — these are the three sides of triangle STB.
common_mistakes: Placing B on the major axis instead of the minor axis.
Writing ST as ae instead of 2ae, forgetting the factor of 2 between the two foci.

steps.label: Apply the equilateral condition
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Equilateral means all three sides are equal — one equation (SB = ST) is enough, since SB = TB automatically.
steps.memory_tip: For an equilateral triangle, squaring one side-equality avoids dealing with square roots.
steps.why: Since SB = TB already holds by symmetry, the single condition SB = ST is enough to express the equilateral triangle; squaring avoids working with square roots.
common_mistakes: Writing three separate equality conditions instead of the one needed (SB = TB is automatic from symmetry).
Forgetting to square (2ae) correctly as 4a²e², not 2a²e².

steps.label: Substitute b² = a²(1 − e²)
steps.margin_note: Third mark. This substitution turns everything into one variable, e.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever both a²e² and b² appear together, substituting b² = a²(1 − e²) reduces the equation to e alone.
steps.why: Replacing b² with a²(1 − e²) removes b entirely, and dividing by a² removes a — leaving a pure equation in e, which is all the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to divide through by a² after substituting, leaving a mix of a² and e terms.

steps.label: Solve for e
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The e² terms cancel almost completely, leaving a one-line equation for e².
steps.memory_tip: e must be a positive fraction less than 1 for a real ellipse — always take the positive square root.
steps.why: The e² terms on the left cancel exactly, leaving 1 = 4e², which solves immediately to the eccentricity of the ellipse.
common_mistakes: Writing the final answer as e² = 1/4 without taking the square root to get e.
Taking the negative square root — eccentricity is always taken as the positive value.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: No marks — the question does not ask for a diagram. The book draws this figure alongside its own answer.
steps.memory_tip: B sits at the top of the minor axis; S and T are the two foci on the major axis, forming the equilateral triangle's base.
steps.why: The picture shows S, T and B joined into a triangle — seeing that all three sides look equal is the visual version of the equilateral condition the algebra proves.
common_mistakes: Drawing B on the major axis instead of at the top of the minor axis.
Drawing the triangle STB as clearly not equilateral (e.g. a very flat or very tall triangle), which misrepresents the result being found.
